mcqs.question: What are the three required parts of a strong answer describing a deliberate principle violation?
options: Name the principle, apologize for breaking it, promise to fix it eventually
Name the principle, describe how well the code performs, list who wrote it
Name the principle, cite an authoritative source that allows exceptions, move on
Name the principle you broke, name the specific constraint that made following it worse, and name what you did instead as an explicit trade-off
mcqs.explanation: The full skeleton requires naming the principle, the concrete constraint that justified the deviation, and the actual choice made, framed as a trade-off rather than a free win. Apologizing, discussing performance or authorship, or citing an external authority don't demonstrate the actual judgment being tested.

mcqs.question: What test distinguishes a genuinely deliberate trade-off from laziness retroactively dressed up as pragmatism?
options: Whether the code passes all existing unit tests
Whether the cost being accepted could be named at decision time, before being challenged, rather than only invented afterward when questioned
Whether the function is shorter than 20 lines
Whether a senior engineer approved the pull request
mcqs.explanation: A real deliberate trade-off comes with the cost already named at the time of the decision; a retrofitted excuse only produces that justification when challenged later. Passing tests, line count, and approval status don't distinguish genuine judgment from an after-the-fact rationalization.

mcqs.question: What makes a code comment useful for flagging a deliberate principle violation to future engineers?
options: A vague `# TODO: refactor this someday` comment with no further detail
No comment at all, since the code should speak for itself
A comment naming the specific trade-off and constraints that justified the decision, so the next engineer can re-evaluate them explicitly if circumstances change
A comment listing every principle that was technically followed elsewhere in the file
mcqs.explanation: The goal is letting a future engineer see the actual constraints that justified the call and re-evaluate them if the situation has changed — a vague TODO or no comment at all leaves that context invisible, and listing unrelated followed principles doesn't address the specific deviation being made here.

mcqs.question: Why is retroactively describing an accidental oversight as a "deliberate trade-off" a risky answer in an interview?
options: Follow-up questions like "what cost did you weigh?" or "would you do it again at 10x scale?" tend to surface the gap, since a real trade-off has ready answers and a retrofitted excuse doesn't
It's risky only because interviewers dislike hearing about mistakes at all
It's risky because oversights are always worse than deliberate violations regardless of context
It's risky because interviewers can verify git blame timestamps in real time
mcqs.explanation: The real risk is that follow-up questions probing for the actual reasoning tend to expose whether the trade-off was truly considered at the time — a genuine deliberate call has substantive answers ready, while a manufactured one doesn't hold up. This isn't about disliking mistakes generally, an oversight isn't inherently worse than a deliberate call, and it's not really about literal git verification.
